claims.text: The initial material is an additively manufactured dual-nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy.
In situ high-resolution TEM coupled with EDS/EELS mapping can elucidate oxidation-driven elemental redistribution in this alloy.
Controlled in situ high-temperature analysis can reveal time-dependent phase and compositional changes during oxidation.
Oxidation at roughly 700–1000 °C in air or controlled oxygen pressure enables real-time observation of these changes.
Nanoprecipitates in the target alloy promote preferential oxidation reactions.
The nanoprecipitates act as reactive sites for oxidation.
Nanoprecipitates alter local diffusion kinetics during oxidation.
High-temperature oxidation of the target alloy selectively oxidizes particular elements.
Titanium is preferentially oxidized in the target alloy.
Oxidation causes depletion of oxidation-sensitive elements such as Ti from the matrix.
Oxidation-sensitive elements or their oxidation products accumulate at or near nanoprecipitate–matrix interfaces.
Selective oxidation and interfacial elemental redistribution influence the formation and stability of the protective oxide scale.
Nanoprecipitate regions will oxidize faster than the surrounding matrix.
Nanoprecipitate regions will exhibit localized compositional shifts, elemental depletion, and accumulation of oxidation products.
Localized compositional changes will correlate with altered oxide-scale morphology and high-temperature performance.
Comparable cast or wrought samples, or unoxidized regions, do not exhibit the same nanoprecipitate-driven elemental redistribution.
The proposed behavior may depend on alloy composition, oxidation temperature, atmosphere, and reproducibility of the precipitate distribution.
Supplementary methods such as atom-probe tomography may be needed to quantify rapid redistribution and relate it to long-term oxidation resistance.
